findings.summary: The `"$@"` golden rule is stated on page 1, but positional parameters and `$@` are not introduced until page 2.
findings.evidence: Page 1 closing callout: "Golden rule — Always write `\"$@\"` with quotes. Bare `$@` word-splits and glob-expands every argument you were handed." Page 2 is where `$@` is first defined: "`$#` = count of args passed to the function" and the table row "`\"$@\"` — N quoted words".
findings.fix: Move the golden-rule callout (and the preceding `main "$@"` snippet) to page 2, directly under the `$@` versus `$*` table, so the rule lands after the reader knows what `$@` expands to.

findings.summary: `$?` is used as a working tool on pages 2, 3 and 8 but is not defined until page 10.
findings.evidence: Page 2: "fetch_cfg; rc=$?    # capture on the NEXT line" / "echo done           # this would overwrite $?". The definition appears only on page 10: "`$?` = status of the ==most recent foreground command==" / "One slot only — it is **overwritten**, never stacked".
findings.fix: Add the one-line definition of `$?` (status of the most recent foreground command, single slot, overwritten by any command) to the "Reading `$?`" block on page 2 before the capture example; page 10 can then expand on it rather than introduce it.

findings.summary: Page 4 explains lost state, forks and pipeline subshells before "subshell" is defined at the end of page 5.
findings.evidence: Page 4 relies on the concept throughout: flow diagram "caller → fork subshell → f runs → stdout back → vars lost", "A pipe puts `mapfile` in a subshell — array vanishes", and "`f | while read ...` runs the `while` in a subshell under Bash defaults". The definition arrives only at the end of page 5: "A forked copy of the shell process / Inherits all state; nothing it changes flows back".
findings.fix: Move the three-bullet subshell definition (forked copy, inherits state, nothing flows back) to the top of page 4's "Capture Forks" section, leaving the fork/no-fork card table and loss table on pages 5–6 as the expansion.

findings.summary: The `pipefail` comment states the wrong rule — pipefail yields the *last* (rightmost) non-zero status, not the first.
findings.fix: Change the comment to `# last (rightmost) non-zero wins`, and keep the `PIPESTATUS[0]` line as the way to recover an earlier stage's status (e.g. `gen`'s when both `gen` and `sink` fail).

findings.summary: `f && g` is listed as a context where errexit is suppressed, but the command following the final `&&` is explicitly NOT exempt from `set -e`.
findings.evidence: "errexit is suppressed for any command in a condition" / "That means `if f`, `f && g`, `! f`"
findings.fix: Qualify it: in `f && g` only `f` runs with errexit off — `g`, as the command after the final `&&`, still aborts the shell on failure. Bash's rule is "part of any command executed in a && or || list except the command following the final && or ||". Replace the bullet with `` `if f`, `while f`, `! f`, and every command in a `&&`/`||` list except the last ``.

findings.summary: Page titles are offset from the material they sit on for pages 7–9, so the mistakes list and cheat sheet appear under the wrong headings.
findings.evidence: Page 9 is titled "Common Mistakes and Their Fixes" but its blocks are all design rules — "One function, one job", "Name it `verb_noun`", "Skeleton to Memorise", "Run `shellcheck`", the portability table. The actual mistakes ("Unquoted `$@` splits...", "`return \"$str\"` gives 'numeric argument required'", "'command not found' — called above its definition") are on page 8, titled "Recursion, Composition, Call Mechanics", whose recursion material (`fact()`, `FUNCNEST`, `FUNCNAME` stack, dispatch) actually sits on page 7 under "Errors, Traps and Strict Mode".
findings.fix: Re-title pages 7–9 to match the content that dominates each: page 7 → "Recursion and Call Mechanics", page 8 → "Common Mistakes and Their Fixes", page 9 → "Design Rules and Cheat Sheet"; or re-split the blocks so each titled page carries its own chapter.

findings.summary: Claims an empty `$tmp` turns the cleanup trap into `rm -rf /`, which is false for the quoted `rm -rf "$tmp"` shown two blocks earlier.
findings.evidence: "Empty `$tmp` turns it into `rm -rf /`" (trap shown is `trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT`)
findings.fix: With `$tmp` empty, `rm -rf "$tmp"` expands to `rm -rf ""` and just errors (`cannot remove ''`); unquoted `rm -rf $tmp` expands to bare `rm -rf` and removes nothing. The real hazard is a trailing slash or glob — `rm -rf "$tmp"/` or `rm -rf $tmp/*` — which targets `/`. Reword to: "Empty `$tmp` plus a trailing slash (`rm -rf \"$tmp\"/`) targets `/` — guard with `[[ -n $tmp ]] && rm -rf -- \"$tmp\"`."

findings.summary: The Q&A callout's lead-in label renders only a few pixels tall, making it illegible and letting it collide with the question heading above it.
findings.evidence: A grey micro-label reading "Ans→" sits at the left margin directly under "Why did f my file.txt see two arguments?" (pt.2) and under "Why does local fail at the top of my script?" (pt.5), rendered at roughly 4-5px against the page's ~20px body text, touching the descenders of the heading line.
findings.fix: Either drop the "Ans→" marker from the Q&A callout template or render it at the same size as the list text below it and give it clearance from the heading's baseline.

findings.summary: Page 1 shows the `main "$@"` entry-point idiom with no reason given; the definition-order problem it solves is only explained on page 8.
findings.evidence: Page 1: "main() { setup; run \"$@\"; }" / "main \"$@\"     # last line of the file", with no surrounding text. Page 8 supplies the rationale: "Define functions at the top, or wrap in `main` called last" / "A straight-line script runs definitions in order — nothing hoists".
findings.fix: Either attach the one-line rationale ("definitions must run before the call — `main` last guarantees it") to the page 1 snippet, or drop the snippet and keep the idiom on page 8 where it is explained.

findings.summary: The word in the $0 cell of the positional-parameter diagram is wider than the cell and its glyphs run into the cell borders.
findings.evidence: The leftmost stack cell holds "$0" over "script", and "script" spans the full cell width with its first and last letters meeting the vertical cell rules.
findings.fix: Widen the $0 cell or reduce the label font size so the text has horizontal padding inside its box.

findings.summary: `local` appears in page 2's argument examples with no explanation of what it does; its scoping meaning is only given on pages 4–5.
findings.evidence: Page 2: "local name=\"${1:-anon}\"   # unset OR empty" and "local f=\"${1:?path required}\"  # abort+msg", with no gloss. The definition comes on page 4 ("`local x` covers the function and everything it calls") and page 5.
findings.fix: Add a single parenthetical at the first use on page 2 — e.g. "`local` keeps the variable inside this call; full rules on the scope page" — so the keyword is not silent when the reader meets it.

findings.summary: The helper `die` is called on page 2 but not defined until page 7.
findings.evidence: Page 2: "(( rc == 2 )) && die 'bad input'". Page 7 defines it: "die() { printf '%s\\n' \"$*\" >&2; exit 1; }".
findings.fix: Either use an inline `printf ... >&2; return 1` on page 2, or add a one-line note that `die` is the standard fatal-error helper defined on the errors page.

findings.summary: `IFS` is referenced in the `$@` versus `$*` table without ever being defined, and the `IFS[0]` notation reads as array indexing.
findings.evidence: Page 2 table row: "`\"$*\"` — one word, joined by `IFS[0]`". `IFS` appears only once more, unexplained, in page 6's strict header: "IFS=$'\\n\\t'   # no space-splitting".
findings.fix: Write the row as "one word, joined by the first character of `IFS` (the field separator, a space by default)".

findings.summary: A connector line in the scope flowchart runs straight through the "can overwrite it" node instead of stopping at its border.
findings.evidence: In the dashed "main: local tmp" diagram, the vertical edge leaving "build -> pack" crosses the top border of the "can overwrite it" box and continues over its label toward "also sees tmp".
findings.fix: Re-route the edge around the node (or terminate it at the node border) so no connector is drawn over box text.
Fine if the two pages cover different topics; rename if they do not.

findings.summary: The FUNCNAME stack diagram puts `main` below `source`, but `main` is always the highest-indexed element of FUNCNAME.
findings.evidence: matrix rows `["[2] main","[3] source"]` under caption "FUNCNAME"
findings.fix: Swap the two cells so the stack reads `[0] fact`, `[1] compute`, `[2] source`, `[3] main` — per the Bash manual, "the bottom-most element (the one with the highest index) is `main`".

findings.summary: The portability table labels the `function` keyword, arrays and `[[ ]]` as "Bash only" when all three also exist in ksh (where they originated) and zsh.
findings.fix: Change both cells to "not POSIX; Bash/ksh/zsh" — the actionable point is that they break under `dash`/`sh`, not that Bash is the only shell with them.

findings.summary: The pushpin on the yellow annotation overlaps the last characters of the code line above it.
findings.evidence: In the bottom-right code block, the pin graphic of the note "copy it before anything else runs" sits on top of the tail of the line "(( rc == 0 )) || die 'backup'".
findings.fix: Offset the pinned note down (or the pin left) so the note's decoration clears the final code line's bounding box.

findings.summary: The pushpin on the "any command overwrites $?" note overlaps the comment text of the code line above it.
findings.evidence: The pin sits over the code line "echo $?    # log's status!", landing between "log's" and "status!".
findings.fix: Move the pinned note below the code block's last line so the pin does not intersect the comment text.
